newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Lebanon vote step forward despite flaws.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Lebanon vote step forward despite flaws.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday that the staging of parliamentary elections in Lebanon was a step forward for the country despite what it called "significant flaws" in the vote.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns pointed to what he called a "relatively smooth process" in the five-stage elections and significantly increased voter participation compared with a previous vote in 1992.

These features, he said, underscored "the great desire of the Lebanese people to put the war years behind them, to focus on rebuilding their nation economically and politically, and (on) advancing the cause of national reconciliation".
"Despite significant flaws, we believe that these elections represent a step forward for Lebanon," Burns told a news briefing. "So we're very pleased that these elections took place."

The U.S. spokesman made no comment on the results of the elections, in which supporters of the pro-Syrian government emerged comfortably in control of the 128-member house, with the number of opposition deputies reduced from 12 to seven.
He also declined to expand on the "flaws", saying allegations of fraud were for Lebanese authorities and international monitors to investigate.

Burns said Secretary of State Warren Christopher had developed a "very good relationship" with Lebanese President Elias Hrawi and Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, and Washington looked forward to further contacts with them.
Christopher paid a flying visit to Lebanon last April as part of a shuttle to arrange a ceasefire in south Lebanon between Israel and pro-Iranian Hizbollah guerrillas.

Despite occasional visits to Lebanon by U.S. officials, Washington maintains a nominal ban on travel there by ordinary Americans because of what it sees as a security threat. U.S. authorities, however, turn a blind eye to visits to Lebanon by tens of thousands of Americans every year.
